Greetings! Today, I would like to briefly go over one of my favorite and seemingly lesser-known Python modules. The collections module (Python 2) contains a few use ful container objects that when implemented in the right scenerios will speed up your code while also making it more readable. Python 3 added a few more that aren't in Python 2 which I'm not fully familiar with yet, so I would like to just go over one of the objects I use that is common to both versions of Python.

The examples below will also utilize the namedtuple object I described in PART 1 of this series. If you are unfamiliar with it, please read that before continuing.

 

collections.deque -- "Deques are a generalization of stacks and queues (the name is pronounced "deck" and is short for "double-ended queue").

The deque object is very similar to a list. It is mutable and supports many of the same methods like append, extend, and insert. Where the deque really shines in comparison is in its efficiency when you want to append or pop from either side of the deque. There are append and pop methods for adding or removing items from the "right" side, or end of the deque. There are also the appendleft and popleft methods for adding or removing items from the "left" side, or beginning of the deque.

The deque is pretty much a drop-in replacement for any list. Most of the time a list is sufficient, but if you want to do a lot of popping, inserting, and/or use threading, a deque is the way to go. The example below will be preparing a deck of standard playing cards using a deque for the deck and namedtuples for the cards.

>>> from collections import deque, namedtuple
>>> import itertools
>>> import random

>>> suits = ('Hearts', 'Diamonds', 'Spades', 'Clubs')
>>> values = itertools.chain(range(2, 11), ('Jack', 'Queen', 'King', 'Ace'))
>>> PlayingCard = namedtuple('PlayingCard', ('value', 'suit'))
>>> deck = deque()

To start out, I made a tuple with card suit strings for building the deck with. In the next line, I used itertools.chain to chain together the range object and a tuple with the face card values. That function turns multiple iterables into a single iterable and can be very handy for when you might want to iterate over two or more different types of iterables all at once. Then the PlayingCard namedtuple was defined with the values of "suit" and "value" for the card's suit and number/face. Now I'll prepare the deck for use.

>>> for value in values:
 for suit in suits:
 deck.append(PlayingCard(value, suit))

>>> random.shuffle(deck)
>>> len(deck)
52

Now the deck is ready to be used. It has all 52 cards and has been shuffled with the random module's shuffle function. That function shuffles an iterable in place, which is perfect for this use case. Since performance is the same either way, I'm going to use the "right" of the deque as the bottom and the "left" as the top.

>>> drawn_card = deck.popleft()
>>> print(drawn_card)
PlayingCard(value=9, suit='Spades')
>>> len(deck)
51

A single card is drawn from the top of deck (popped from the left of the deque), which its new len reflects. The card object is referenced by the drawn_card variable. When you pop or popleft not only is the item removed from the deque, but you can assign it to a variable for doing whatever with it.

>>> deck.append(drawn_card)
>>> len(deck)
52
>>> print(deck[-1])
PlayingCard(value=9, suit='Spades')
>>> deck.index(drawn_card)
51

The card has been added to the bottom of the deck. Just for fun, let's draw a hand of five cards now.

>>> hand = [deck.popleft() for card in range(5)]
>>> print(hand)
[PlayingCard(value=7, suit='Spades'), PlayingCard(value='Jack', suit='Spades'), PlayingCard(value=7, suit='Hearts'), PlayingCard(value='King', suit='Spades'), PlayingCard(value=4, suit='Spades')]

So there you have it, just one simple use for the deque. Let me know if this guide was helpful and/or well-written enough. If so, you can count on there being a part three some time in the near future. I'll be glad to answer any questions about this guide or deques. Also, I'm considering covering itertools once I've finished this module. Let me know what you think about that or if you know of another standard library module you would like to see covered. Thanks for reading, and happy coding!
